onboarding.metaTitle: First sign-in — export your listening data
onboarding.welcomeBullet1: Pick Spotify or Apple Music—every screen stays on your choice.
onboarding.welcomeBullet2: Follow screenshots to request the official listening export.
onboarding.welcomeBullet3: Upload when the email arrives—most exports land within a few days.
onboarding.whyNotApiSummary: Why upload a file instead of a sync button?
onboarding.whyNotApiTitle: Why can’t this app connect to Apple Music or Spotify for me?
onboarding.whyNotApiBody: Those companies don’t give independent apps direct access to your personal listening history — that data stays between you and them, which protects your privacy. We’re a third-party app, so there’s no supported “log in and sync” path for your full history. The official option is for you to request your own copy from their privacy tools; you then import that file here.
onboarding.welcomeBody: Charts run on rows parsed from exports you approve—not a fuzzy “music login”. Start the wizard now; you can pause anywhere and reopen this page when your download is ready.
onboarding.welcomeNoteStrong: You'll import when the ZIP or CSV arrives in your inbox
onboarding.welcomeNoteRest: — exports take time to generate, and that's OK.
onboarding.pickSubtitle: One path keeps the guide coherent—everything below matches Apple or Spotify, not both.
onboarding.pickSpotifyHint: Extended streaming history with curated screenshots.
onboarding.pickAppleHint: Apple Media Services archive with curated screenshots.

spotify.step1Body: On the “Download your data” page, select Extended streaming history, then tap “Request data.” Account data may arrive sooner, but extended history is usually richer; Spotify may take up to 30 days to prepare it.
spotify.step2Body: On “Account privacy,” a green banner confirms Spotify is preparing your file. You will get an email when the download is ready.

apple.step1Title: Request a copy of your data
apple.step1Body: Sign in to Apple’s Data & Privacy portal, then under “Manage your data,” open “Request a copy of your data.”
apple.step2Body: In the list, check “Apple Media Services Information” (App Store, Apple Music, Podcasts, etc.). You can leave other categories unchecked for a focused export.
apple.step3Body: Pick a maximum file size that is easy for you to download — 1 GB is usually fine. Review the summary, then complete the request.
apple.step4Body: Apple thanks you and explains that preparation can take up to several days; you will be notified at your Apple ID email.
apple.step5Body: When the archive is ready, Apple emails the address on your Apple ID. Open the message and use the link (for example “Get your data”) to go to your downloads page and fetch the Apple Media Services package.
apple.step6Body: On Apple’s “Download your data” page, download each part of the archive (Apple may split it into multiple files, e.g. part 1 of 2). Links expire after a limited time — save the files somewhere safe before you unzip.
apple.step7Body: Open each downloaded .zip (double-click on Mac, or extract on Windows). You should get a top-level folder named Apple_Media_Services — that is the package to open in the next step.
apple.step8Body: Inside Apple_Media_Services, open the folder Apple Music Activity (see first screenshot). Then select Apple Music - Play History Daily Tracks.csv (second screenshot) — this is the file you will upload here; we do not import other CSVs from the export.

import.spotifyBody: Download the file you were sent and upload it in the app as a .zip archive.
import.appleBody: Upload Apple Music - Play History Daily Tracks.csv — the file from the last step of the guide above. We only read this CSV from your export.

insights.title: Insights & methodology
insights.subtitle: Understand what each page reveals, how analytics are calculated, and where the current limitations are. Use this as a reference to import data and get more value from the dashboard.

summary.patterns: Patterns: Overview surfaces KPIs plus embedded summaries; Library covers tracks/artists, trend pages, and genre palette; Timeline/heatmap/temporal analysis explore rhythm; AI adds Ask your Soundprint, AI Insights, musical profile, and taste evolution. Account tools (live Spotify, API playground, settings) and the demo videos sit beside that core—they inform or operate the product but do not replace export-backed history.
summary.calculations: Calculations: PostgreSQL aggregations (daily/weekly/monthly), global stats, genre cascade (Track → ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP → Unknown), and CSV/JSON/PDF exports.
summary.limitations: Limitations: Genre mapping coverage, source-data completeness, live Spotify API vs export-backed history, estimated listen time, query performance at scale, and artist/track normalization.
summary.architecture: Architecture: Next.js App Router, PostgreSQL + Prisma, Redis (optional, ioredis) plus TanStack Query, Groq-backed AI with server-side insight caching, Recharts, Spotify/Apple-first ingestion (Last.fm optional).

overview.title: Your Music
overview.paragraph: The /dashboard/overview page is the main snapshot: headline KPIs versus the prior window of the same length, a recent-listens area chart, and links into deeper views. It also embeds summary widgets—heatmap preview, genre/artist/track momentum cards, taste profile teaser, an AI insights excerpt, top artists, and expandable per-artist breakdowns aligned with the artists area. Related routes include /dashboard/tracks, /dashboard/artists, /dashboard/musical-profile, and this methodology page at /dashboard/insights.

timeline.title: Timeline and Temporal Trends
timeline.paragraph: The /dashboard/timeline and /dashboard/genres/trends pages reveal listening cycles with aggregation by day, week or month:
timeline.li1: Weekly cycles: Days of the week when you listen the most
timeline.li2: Seasonal variations: Monthly evolution of habits
timeline.li3: Genre trends: Genres on the rise or decline over the period (first vs second half comparison)

heatmap.title: Listening Heatmap
heatmap.paragraph: The /dashboard/heatmap page displays a GitHub-style calendar with listening intensity per day. It identifies your most active days and distribution by day of the week.

temporal.title: Advanced Temporal Analysis
temporal.paragraph: The /dashboard/temporal-analysis page details your listening patterns: listens by day of the week (Monday-Sunday), by hour of the day, and identifies peak moments (day and hour when you listen the most).

genres.title: Genre Diversity and Preferences
genres.paragraph: The /dashboard/genres, /dashboard/genres/trends, and /dashboard/genres/palette pages reveal the extent of your musical palette: dominant genres, temporal evolution, diversity metrics, and a dedicated palette visualization. Unique artists and unique tracks highlight the balance between repetition and exploration.

libraryTrends.title: Track and artist trend views
libraryTrends.paragraph: Beyond the high-level genre summaries, /dashboard/tracks/trends and /dashboard/artists/trends chart listen volume across the filtered range using day, week, or month buckets—so you can follow specific tracks or your top artists over time. They honor the same global date filter as the rest of the dashboard.

ai.title: AI-Powered Insights
ai.paragraph: Several experiences use Groq-hosted models on top of your analytics summary and listening data:
ai.li1: /dashboard/ask-your-soundprint: Conversational assistant with tool-backed answers over your library (honors the dashboard date filter)
ai.li2: /dashboard/ai-insights: Short natural-language insight cards (optional; requires Groq credentials server-side)
ai.li3: /dashboard/musical-profile: Enriches your stats with an AI-generated musical identity
ai.li4: /dashboard/taste-evolution: Week-to-week taste shifts with AI commentary
ai.li5: Repeated AI insight requests reuse a 24h server cache when REDIS_URL is configured (in-memory fallback in local dev) so identical inputs do not always call the model again.

dateRange.title: Date Range Filter
dateRange.paragraph: The top filter scopes analytics to presets (7 days, 30 days, year-to-date, custom range) or all time. For the all-time preset, the client resolves the true min/max listen dates from /api/date-range so features such as AI insights and taste profile use your full history instead of silently falling back to a short default window. Exports (CSV, JSON, PDF) honor the selected range.

accountTooling.title: Account: live Spotify, API playground, and settings
accountTooling.paragraph: The Account section of the sidebar is deliberately separate from the export-backed analytics storyline. /dashboard/spotify-snapshot shows what the Spotify Web API returns today—profile, top tracks and artists, recently played—so you can compare that live snapshot with the long-term rows in your Listen table built from imports. That route can be used once Spotify is OAuth-linked even when full export onboarding is incomplete; it reflects API state, not your warehouse. /dashboard/spotify-playground is the same family of endpoints in raw JSON form for debugging scopes and payloads; it is operational tooling, not a listening-history dashboard. /dashboard/settings collects preferences, confirmations, and safety actions (such as deletion): they change your experience and account state, not how historical aggregates are defined from stored plays.

productDemo.title: Walkthrough videos (demo)
productDemo.paragraph: /dashboard/demo embeds product walkthrough videos for orientation and storytelling. Treat them as illustrative—they are not ingested as data, and every personalized chart still derives from listens stored in your account.

aggregations.title: Temporal Aggregations
aggregations.paragraph: Aggregations use native PostgreSQL SQL (via Prisma) for performance:
aggregations.li1: Daily: date bucket from the Listen.playedAt timestamp
aggregations.li2: Weekly: DATE_TRUNC('week', playedAt) buckets ISO weeks (Monday start)
aggregations.li3: Monthly: calendar month bucket from playedAt (typically YYYY-MM)
aggregations.li4: Counts: COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT ...) on listens, tracks, and artists as needed

stats.title: Global Statistics
stats.paragraph: Your Music statistics are calculated as follows:
stats.li1: Total listens: Total count of records in the Listen table
stats.li2: Unique artists: Distinct count of artist_id via listened tracks
stats.li3: Unique tracks: Distinct count of track_id
stats.li4: Total time: Sum of track durations (in seconds) for all listens

genres.title: Genre Distribution
genres.paragraph: Genres follow a cascade resolution with priority:
genres.li1: 1. Track.genre: Genre stored on the track (from Last.fm when available on import)
genres.li2: 2. ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP: Static manual mapping by artist name (fallback if Track.genre is null)
genres.li4: Listens are aggregated by resolved genre; percentages are calculated on total listens

export.title: Data Export
export.paragraph: Exports are available in the filter bar (CSV, JSON, PDF icons):
export.li1: CSV: All listens with Date, Artist, Title, Genre, Source (period filters applied)
export.li2: JSON: Aggregated statistics (overview, timeline, genres) in structured format
export.li3: PDF: Custom annual report with charts and top artists/tracks per year

genreMapping.title: Genre Mapping
genreMapping.limitation: The ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP fallback only covers a handful of popular artists. Tracks without genre in the database remain classified as "Unknown" when neither Track.genre nor the map provides a value.
genreMapping.impact: Some artists/tracks may appear as "Unknown", reducing the fineness of genre analysis.
genreMapping.solution: Use Last.fm genres when present on imported tracks, or extend ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP for additional artists.

dataSources.title: Data Sources
dataSources.limitation: For the public product, primary ingestion is based on user-requested exports (Spotify ZIP + Apple Music CSV). Last.fm remains legacy/optional and is no longer expected in the default UX path.
dataSources.impact: The main risk is missing or stale export files, not missing Last.fm scrobbles. Coverage depends on what users actually request and upload.
dataSources.solution: Design onboarding and in-app prompts around export-import flows; treat Last.fm as an advanced fallback for power users only.

liveSpotifyApi.title: Live Spotify Web API
liveSpotifyApi.limitation: Snapshot and playground calls reflect Spotify's current API rules—time windows, limits, and how "top" or "recent" lists are defined—not the same completeness or replay semantics as a user-requested account export ingested into Listen.
liveSpotifyApi.impact: Side-by-side comparison with your warehouse can diverge (e.g. recency filters, listening not exposed through these endpoints, curated tops vs. full history in exports).
liveSpotifyApi.solution: Use live API views for debugging or quick checks; rely on imported listens for longitudinal dashboards, exports, and like-for-like historical analysis.

listenTime.title: Listen Time Calculation
listenTime.limitation: Total listening time is estimated by summing track durations, without accounting for interruptions or partial listens.
listenTime.impact: Calculated time may overestimate actual listening time if tracks are often interrupted or partially listened.
listenTime.solution: Possible improvement: Use playback progress data if available in sources.

queryPerformance.title: Query Performance
queryPerformance.limitation: Trade-off: Complex aggregations require loading listens into memory for calculations.
queryPerformance.impact: Performance may degrade with very large datasets (millions of listens).
queryPerformance.solution: Possible optimizations: Materialized views, additional indexes, or asynchronous calculations for large data.

dataNormalization.title: Data Normalization
dataNormalization.limitation: Normalization of artist and track names depends on exact string matching.
dataNormalization.impact: Name variants (e.g. "The Weeknd" vs "Weeknd") may create duplicate entries in statistics.
dataNormalization.solution: Possible improvement: Use MusicBrainz identifiers (MBID) or fuzzy matching algorithms for deduplication.

stack.title: Technology Stack
stack.li1: Backend: Next.js (App Router) with API Routes
stack.li3: Cache: optional Redis (REDIS_URL, ioredis; Upstash-compatible TLS) for AI insight caching plus TanStack Query on the client
stack.li4: Frontend: React 18, TanStack Query v5, Tailwind CSS, Sonner (toasts)
stack.li7: AI/LLM: Groq for generated copy and conversational analytics; insight responses cached server-side (~24h TTL) when Redis is available

model.title: Data Model
model.li1: Artist: name, nameLower (case-insensitive search), MBID, imageUrl
model.li2: Track: title, artist, duration, genre (Last.fm when available), MBID
model.li3: Listen: timestamp (playedAt), source (spotify_export | apple_music_export | apple_music_replay | lastfm), link to Track

import.title: Data Import
import.li1: Primary path (public): user imports from onboarding flows (Spotify export ZIP and Apple Music export CSV), then data is parsed and stored account-side.
import.li2: Secondary path (legacy): Last.fm sync via scripts/API remains available for advanced usage, but is intentionally de-emphasized for UX.

spotifyPlayground.apiTroubleshootTitle: Seeing errors on Top tracks / Top artists / Recently played?
spotifyPlayground.apiTroubleshootBody:
• OAuth scopes: Top and recently-played need user-top-read and user-read-recently-played. In Supabase, open Authentication → Providers → Spotify and set the provider scopes to include those (same string as SPOTIFY_WEB_API_OAUTH_SCOPES in your app). Then sign out and sign in with Spotify again.
• HTTP 502 / 500 / “Server error”: Spotify sometimes has short outages — wait and tap Reload. If /v1/me works but other tabs fail, check scopes first.

brandCard.title: Soundprint-AI
brandCard.lead: A personal analytics space for your Apple Music and Last.fm history—trends, habits, and insights in one calm dashboard.

whatIs.title: What is this?
whatIs.paragraph: Soundprint-AI is a personal dashboard that visualizes your listening habits over time. You can ingest data from Last.fm scrobbles or Apple Music CSV exports, then explore stats, trends, and insights in one place.

whyLastfm.title: Why Last.fm instead of Apple Music?
whyLastfm.paragraph: The official Apple Music API requires a paid developer membership and may introduce usage costs. Last.fm is a practical free source for personal projects, and CSV imports provide a fallback when you want to backfill history.

whatIsLastfm.title: What is Last.fm?
whatIsLastfm.paragraph: Last.fm is a music service that tracks your listens across platforms (Apple Music, Spotify, and more). Each scrobble includes metadata like artist, track, and timestamp. This project fetches that history and stores it locally for analytics.

workflow.title: How does the data get here?

steps.step1: Listen to music — Use Apple Music (or any supported app) on your phone as usual.
steps.step2: Last.fm scrobbling — Last.fm is linked to your Apple Music account and automatically records each listen.
steps.step3: Capture and sync — New listens are sent to Last.fm via scrobbling, or imported later from Apple Music CSV exports.
steps.step4: Update the database — Run the update/import scripts to fetch fresh listens and store them in your local database.
steps.step5: Dashboard refreshes — Once the data pipeline completes, charts and metrics reflect the newest records.
steps.step6: Data looks stale? — Most of the time, it means no recent sync/import has run yet.
